newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-East German leader says regrets wall killings.
newsitem.headline: Ex-East German leader says regrets wall killings.

text.p: East Germany's last orthodox Communist leader said on Thursday he regretted he had been unable to stop a policy of shooting people as they tried to flee to the West but the practice was inevitable in the Cold War climate.

"It is a personal defeat of my life that I could not prevent deaths and injuries on the border. But it would be dishonest to say we could have stopped it," Egon Krenz told a court trying him and two others for the killings.
More than 800 people died along German border barriers trying to flee the communist East during a half century of Cold War that split Europe until 1989.

Krenz, answering the Berlin court for the first time in the year-and-a-half-long trial, rejected the charges of responsibility for deaths of East Germans trying to flee over the old Berlin Wall or inter-German border.
He argued that the leaders of former communist East Germany, which was absorbed by West Germany through unification in 1990, had not formally authorised the killings on the fortified border.
Krenz denied there was a specific order to kill people trying to cross the border and said each death and injury had deeply upset him.

Krenz, who led East Germany for just three weeks in 1989 after longtime leader Erich Honecker resigned in the face of mass pro-democracy demonstrations, said the reason for the deaths was the East-West conflict and no East German leader or institution could have changed that.
Earlier on Thursday, the German supreme court upheld a Berlin court verdict that six former East German generals were guilty of ordering border guards to shoot people trying to escape to the West.

The Berlin court had sentenced the six officers to between three years and three months and more than six years in jail last year for 15 counts of manslaughter and attempted manslaughter between 1980 and 1989.
Krenz, 60, said he had personally campaigned for the East German media to publish details of the deaths on the border. "That way I wanted to prevent people getting into trouble," he said.
Two of Krenz's deputies -- Guenter Schabowski and Guenther Kleiber -- are also on trial for manslaughter.

Krenz alleges that then-West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev agreed in 1990 that no East German leaders would be prosecuted if they had not broken the law of their own country.
Krenz said the trial was political and illegal but he assumed he would be condemned. The prosecution and defence are now expected to begin summing up.
